strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: obtaining useful natural-language supervision for fine-grained biological vision models when instance-level captions are unavailable.

The proposed pipeline is practical and scalable, combining Wikipedia-derived morphology, taxon-specific examples, and an MLLM to caption roughly 10 million images. Prompts, compute requirements, training hyperparameters, and coverage statistics are documented in substantial detail.

The empirical results are broad and consistently positive. BIOCAP improves over BIOCLIP across ten classification tasks and performs strongly on INQUIRE-Rerank and two biological retrieval benchmarks.

The TreeOfLife-1M ablations provide useful evidence for the contribution of trait-focused prompting, format examples, Wikipedia context, and separate projectors. The covered/non-covered-species experiment also suggests some transfer beyond taxa directly represented in Wikipedia.

Caption quality is evaluated on 200 taxonomically diverse images with randomized presentation, two judgments per image, multiple criteria, and reported inter-rater agreement. Qualitative localization and embedding analyses complement the quantitative results.
The work has potentially high practical value: releasing the captions and model could provide a useful resource for biodiversity and organismal-vision research.
weaknesses: The central claim that descriptive traits provide benefits "beyond labels" is not fully isolated. Every synthetic caption is explicitly required to contain the species name, so improvements may partly arise from repeating or contextualizing label identity rather than from visible traits. Essential controls include captions with species names removed, repeated/name-templated label supervision matched for the number of text views, and shuffled or mismatched trait descriptions.

The headline comparison with BIOCLIP does not clearly provide a full-scale, identically trained label-only baseline. The controlled ablations use TreeOfLife-1M and different training settings, whereas the main BIOCAP model uses TreeOfLife-10M. No multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, making it difficult to separate caption effects from recipe and run variance.

The two newly collected retrieval benchmarks are insufficiently specified. The manuscript gives little detail about collection, filtering, candidate pools, train-pretraining overlap, duplicate handling, or whether relevance is defined at the exact-pair or species level. Because training captions and evaluation descriptions may encode the same species-level facts, the very large retrieval gains may not demonstrate instance-level grounding as strongly as claimed.

The human evaluation validates relative preference rather than factual correctness. Fifteen of sixteen evaluators are computer-science students rather than biological experts, captions are selected in a forced best-of-three format without ties or absolute ratings, and only one image per taxonomic class is assessed. The striking 85% win rate could partly reflect stylistic consistency, terminology, or caption length.

The theoretical analysis is mainly an intuition under restrictive linear-Gaussian assumptions. It does not establish that real generated captions suppress nuisance variables, and the Grad-CAM and t-SNE examples are selectively qualitative evidence rather than a rigorous test of this causal claim.

The method is evaluated with only one captioning MLLM. Errors from genus-level descriptions, taxonomic coverage bias, and performance variation across taxa or demographic forms are not analyzed sufficiently, despite their relevance to biological deployment and the stated fidelity motivation.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: obtaining useful natural-language supervision for fine-grained biological representation learning at large scale.
The proposed pipeline is practical and clearly described, combining taxon-specific examples, Wikipedia-derived morphology, and MLLM captioning for roughly 10 million images.
Reported improvements over BIOCLIP are large across classification and retrieval, and the paper includes several ablations, qualitative visualizations, and a caption preference study.
Prompts, model configurations, compute requirements, and major training hyperparameters are documented in substantial detail.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not isolate the central claim that instance-grounded captions are responsible for the gains. Captions are generated using the ground-truth species name and external species-level knowledge, and every caption repeats that name. Missing controls include captions generated without the image, captions shuffled within a species, label paraphrases, and attribute-only species descriptions. Consequently, gains may reflect duplicated labels, text augmentation, or external knowledge rather than instance-specific visual grounding.

The newly collected Cornell Bird and PlantID retrieval benchmarks are inadequately specified. The paper does not describe train-test overlap or duplicate-image checks, candidate-pool construction, relevance definitions, or whether query text contains species names. With approximately 10 images per Cornell species and three per PlantID species, Recall@10 can be strongly confounded by species-name matching and may not measure the claimed fine-grained instance understanding.

Caption validation is too weak for the claimed biological fidelity. Fifteen of sixteen annotators are computer-science students, evaluation is forced-choice rather than absolute, only one ecologist participates, and no expert-written reference captions or competitive captioning systems are included. Fluency and extra detail can therefore win even when subtle biological claims are incorrect.

Several comparisons and ablations are insufficiently controlled. Main results provide no uncertainty over seeds, ablations use the smaller TreeOfLife-1M setup rather than the reported 10M training regime, the individual effect of Wikipedia context is not cleanly separated from format examples, and baseline training/data matching is not documented well enough to establish strict fairness.

The theoretical section is largely post-hoc intuition. Its linear-Gaussian assumptions and covariance decomposition do not prove that InfoNCE recovers the latent trait vector or suppresses nuisance information, while the manuscript presents these conclusions more strongly than the analysis supports.

Novelty is limited relative to established synthetic-caption CLIP training: the main additions are domain-specific prompt/context construction and a previously used separated-projector design. The scale is valuable, but the missing causal controls and questionable retrieval protocol prevent the empirical contribution from overcoming this limitation.

The reproducibility statement claims released code and data, but the corresponding links are blank in the submitted manuscript, so the central 10-million-caption resource and reported results cannot presently be inspected or reproduced.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored problem: obtaining useful natural-language supervision for fine-grained biological vision models when only taxonomic labels are widely available.

The proposed captioning pipeline is practical and reasonably well motivated, combining image evidence, Wikipedia-derived morphology, and taxon-specific examples. Its scale—roughly 10 million captions spanning a broad taxonomic distribution—is a substantial contribution.

The empirical gains are large and consistent. BIOCAP improves over BIOCLIP by 8.8 points on average across ten zero-shot classification benchmarks and by 21.3 points across the reported natural-language tasks, while also outperforming several general and biological CLIP baselines.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering animals, plants, fungi, camera traps, rare species, retrieval, reranking, human caption assessment, and qualitative localization. The ablations show that naive captions can hurt, trait-focused prompting helps, domain context helps further, and captions transfer benefits to taxa without Wikipedia coverage.

The appendices provide prompts, coverage statistics, compute requirements, hyperparameters, benchmark details, human-evaluation agreement, and qualitative examples. Releasing code, captions, and models would make this a valuable community resource.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are not fully isolated experimentally. The paper lacks a Trait+Wiki ablation, so the separate contribution of Wikipedia context cannot be distinguished from format examples. Likewise, the dual-projector comparison changes model capacity and does not establish that the architectural choice itself—rather than extra parameters—causes the gain.

The natural-language results require stronger controls. The newly collected retrieval benchmarks are insufficiently characterized regarding whether captions contain species names, how multiple images of the same species are treated as positives, and whether images or near-duplicates overlap with TreeOfLife-10M. Species-name matching or leakage could inflate the very large retrieval gains.

Caption validation remains limited relative to a 10M-caption dataset. The forced-choice human study provides no absolute error or hallucination rate, uses only 200 images, and has just one ecologist among 16 evaluators. Some displayed outputs still contain clear artifacts or uncertainty, such as the stray “sci.txt” text and “possibly” species identification despite the supplied label.

The theoretical treatment is mainly intuition rather than a substantive result. It assumes a shared linear nuisance variable and argues from cross-covariance under the favorable condition D=0, without proving that the proposed prompting produces this condition or empirically measuring suppression of spurious correlations. Grad-CAM and t-SNE examples do not establish the claimed causal mechanism.

Results are reported without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Reproducibility details also contain minor inconsistencies, such as AdamW in the text versus Adam in the hyperparameter tables, and do not specify all sampling seeds or the instantiated caption word limit.

Comparison to the strongest recent biological foundation models is incomplete. BIOCLIP 2 is discussed and its benchmarks are adopted, but it is not included as a quantitative baseline; the main comparison is instead to the earlier BIOCLIP trained at a more comparable scale. This limits the strength of state-of-the-art positioning.

The caption-generation pipeline requires substantial compute and manual curation of 896 examples, and its dependence on a single 38B MLLM is not studied. Robustness across captioning models, biological subdomains, and lower-resource generation settings remains unknown.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: exploiting natural-language supervision for organismal biology when available datasets largely contain only taxonomic labels. The proposed use of Wikipedia-derived morphology and taxon-specific examples is intuitive and practically useful.

The empirical results are strong. Relative to BIOCLIP, BIOCAP improves mean zero-shot classification from 37.6 to 46.4 and mean language/retrieval performance from 31.6 to 53.5, with gains across diverse animal, plant, and fungi benchmarks.

The evaluation is unusually broad and includes caption-strategy ablations, projector and compute controls, Wikipedia-covered versus uncovered taxa, multiple caption generators and model sizes, underrepresented species, localization analyses, and human evaluation.

The caption-generation pipeline is described in substantial detail, including prompts, coverage statistics, computational cost, training hyperparameters, benchmark sizes, and retrieval-set leakage filtering. The cross-generator and repeated-example experiments provide useful evidence of robustness.

The comparison between raw Wikipedia text, generic synthetic captions, trait-focused captions, and the complete context-guided method supports the central conclusion that caption quality and grounding matter, rather than arbitrary extra text always helping.
weaknesses: The main comparison does not cleanly isolate descriptive information beyond labels. Trait-focused captions are explicitly required to contain the ground-truth species name, whereas the Base prompt is not. Thus, the large Base-to-Trait and no-caption-to-full-caption gains conflate morphological descriptions, class-conditioned caption generation, and an additional occurrence of the label. A crucial ablation would remove species names from otherwise identical captions or match label exposure across objectives.

The claim that the pipeline produces faithful captions at scale is only weakly validated. Human evaluation covers 200 of roughly 10 million images, uses a forced-choice preference protocol rather than absolute factual-error annotation, and involves only one ecologist among 16 evaluators. Consequently, the reported 82.4% groundedness win rate is relative to weak baselines and is not an estimate of caption accuracy or hallucination prevalence.

The two newly collected retrieval benchmarks are insufficiently characterized. The paper does not clearly specify how their textual descriptions were obtained, whether multiple images or texts correspond to the same species, how instance-level relevance is defined, or how ambiguous valid matches are handled by Recall@10. These details matter because the very large retrieval improvements are central to the paper.

Duplicate filtering is reported for the new retrieval datasets but not for most classification benchmarks. Since TreeOfLife-10M aggregates web and biodiversity-repository images and most classification tasks contain species observed during pretraining, image-level overlap or near-duplicates could inflate the headline zero-shot classification results. Rare Species partially addresses taxonomic generalization but does not replace systematic leakage analysis.

The morphospace and covariance analysis is heuristic rather than a substantive theoretical result. It assumes captions exclude nuisance information, while the proposed captions may explicitly contain substrate and contextual details. Grad-CAM and t-SNE visualizations do not establish the claimed causal mechanism of suppressing spurious correlations.

Reproducibility at the stated scale remains demanding: caption generation uses 12 H100 GPUs and training uses 8 H100 GPUs with a global batch size of 32,768. Exact combined loss weights, sampling between taxonomy and caption paths, and sufficiently detailed construction metadata for the new retrieval sets should also be specified more clearly.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: obtaining scalable, instance-level language supervision for biological foundation models when existing datasets predominantly provide only taxonomic labels.
BIOCAP reports substantial zero-shot gains over BIOCLIP across ten classification tasks and strong improvements on INQUIRE, Cornell Bird, and PlantID retrieval benchmarks.
The empirical study is broad, including caption-strategy, context-source, projector, training-component, caption-generator, model-size, exemplar-count, and generation-stability ablations.

The appendix provides prompts, hyperparameters, computational requirements, coverage statistics, benchmark descriptions, and human-evaluation instructions; the claimed release of captions, models, and code would be a useful resource.
The evaluation includes human caption preferences, localization measurements, underrepresented-species analysis, and comparisons with several general-purpose and biology-specific models.
weaknesses: The decisive full-scale comparison is insufficiently controlled. BIOCAP is compared with an existing BIOCLIP model, while controlled caption-versus-no-caption ablations are conducted only on TreeOfLife-1M under different training settings. Full-scale matched runs, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and compute-matched baselines are missing.

Leakage control is reported only for the two newly collected retrieval datasets, not for the ten classification benchmarks. Because TreeOfLife-10M aggregates images from large biological repositories that may overlap with benchmark sources, the large zero-shot gains cannot be interpreted confidently without image-level and source-level deduplication against every test set.

The retrieval results may reward taxonomic-name matching rather than grounded instance-level understanding: every generated caption is explicitly required to contain the species name, but the paper does not state whether evaluation descriptions contain names, whether candidates share species, or how multiple valid matches are handled. Name-stripped and species-disjoint retrieval evaluations are needed.

The proposed causal and covariance analysis is heuristic. It assumes shared nuisance variables and then asserts that InfoNCE will retain trait directions and discard nuisance directions, but it does not establish this result for normalized nonlinear encoders. The experiments also do not isolate the mechanism using controls such as captions without species names, within-species caption shuffling, or matched generic trait text.

Caption validation is too limited for a corpus of roughly ten million generated captions. Only 200 images are assessed through forced-choice comparison, 15 of the 16 evaluators are computer-science students, no absolute correctness or hallucination rate is measured, and taxonomic or Wikipedia-coverage strata are not audited. A visible generation artifact such as “sci.txt: a photo of Glyceria canadensis” in Figure 9 further suggests imperfect corpus cleaning.

The strongest results are concentrated in zero-shot classification and language retrieval. Few-shot accuracy improves only from 50.0 to 50.5 and 68.5 to 69.1, while the mean across additional biological visual tasks changes from 49.0 to 49.1 and BIOCAP loses on several individual tasks. This weakens claims of generally better visual representations.

The core technical novelty is moderate: synthetic-caption CLIP training and caption refinement with external knowledge or examples are established ideas, and the principal contribution is their carefully engineered application to organismal biology. Given the unresolved evaluation confounds, the evidence falls slightly short of the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically significant contribution: a scalable, domain-grounded caption-generation pipeline for biological foundation-model training, combining Wikipedia-derived visual information with taxon-specific examples.

The empirical results are strong and broad. BIOCAP improves over BIOCLIP by 8.8 percentage points on average across ten zero-shot classification benchmarks and by 21.9 points across natural-language and retrieval evaluations, with particularly large gains on fungi, rare species, and the newly collected retrieval datasets.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough: it studies generic versus trait-focused captions, Wikipedia and exemplar context, single versus dual projectors, additional training epochs, Wikipedia coverage, exemplar count and taxonomic level, caption-generator families and sizes, and independent exemplar-generation rounds.

The authors provide multiple complementary forms of evidence beyond headline accuracy, including human caption assessment, inter-rater agreement, quantitative localization, semantic visualizations, few-shot evaluation, underrepresented-species analysis, and explicit image-level leakage control for the new retrieval benchmarks.

The work is well motivated and clearly presented, with detailed prompts, training hyperparameters, computational requirements, benchmark descriptions, licensing discussion, and an appropriate ethical statement. The planned release of captions, code, and models would constitute a useful community resource.
weaknesses: The main causal attribution is not fully isolated. Generated captions explicitly contain the species name, so improvements over taxonomy-only training may partly reflect repeated or augmented label supervision rather than descriptive traits. A key missing control is a caption branch containing only the species name, or experiments removing or shuffling the species name while preserving descriptive attributes.

The human evaluation is forced-choice rather than an absolute factuality assessment, and only one of the 16 evaluators is an ecologist. Thus, the very high relative win rate establishes preference over weak caption baselines more convincingly than expert-level biological correctness across the long tail of taxa.

The newly collected Cornell Bird and PlantID retrieval benchmarks need more specification regarding how textual descriptions and image-text correspondences were selected, cleaned, and disambiguated. Image deduplication is reported, but possible textual overlap with Wikipedia-derived supervision and contamination of the captioning models are not analyzed.

Most zero-shot headline results appear to come from a single training run without confidence intervals or significance testing. This matters less for the large average gains, but makes smaller ablation differences difficult to interpret reliably.

The morphospace and causal analysis is primarily motivational: assumptions such as independent environmental noise, captions free of nuisance information, and the direction from labels to traits are strong and not empirically validated. Claims that captions suppress spurious correlations should therefore be stated more cautiously.
